content:
The test image shows a corn field where one plant (center-right) has completely wilted and turned brown/tan while the surrounding plants remain healthy and green. Key observations:

- **Affected plant part**: Whole plant (systemic)
- **Color**: Uniform brown/tan discoloration across all leaves
- **Pattern**: Single plant death surrounded by healthy neighbors — classic vascular wilt or stalk rot presentation
- **Tassel**: Visible, also affected/brown
- **No visible leaf spots or pustules** — rules out rust, eyespot, gray leaf spot, etc.

**Reasoning through candidates:**

- **Stewarts_wilt**: Bacterial vascular wilt. In the adult plant blight phase, causes pale-to-tan streaking along leaf blades, progressing to whole-plant wilt/death. Single plant dying while neighbors are healthy is very consistent.
- **Goss_wilt**: Also bacterial wilt — causes water-soaked lesions along veins with bacterial "freckles." Whole plant collapse possible.
- **Diplodia/Charcoal stalk rot**: Stalk rots can cause premature death with leaf "firing," but typically the stalk collapses and plant lodges.

The uniform browning of the entire plant (leaves and tassel) without any discrete spots or lesions, combined with a single plant collapsing while neighbors are unaffected, most strongly points to a systemic vascular wilt. Stewarts_wilt in the adult blight phase is the best match — the leaf tissue is uniformly killed due to blocked vascular flow.
